extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and mathematics students writing papers, lecture notes, or expository proofs (graduate students, researchers, instructors)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and concrete principles for composing clear, effective mathematical prose, proofs, and expository structure aimed at a specified reader (papers, notes, lectures). Emphasizes organization, notation, sentence-level clarity, and revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have something to say
rubrics_metrics.description: Have something to say. The most important ingredient of good exposition is having an important idea worth communicating. Without that, no amount of stylistic polish helps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the significance and clarity of the underlying idea before polishing style; if the idea is weak or trivial, exposition cannot rescue it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address a specific audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Have something to say to a specific audience. Identify the reader explicitly — a beginning graduate student, a working specialist, an undergraduate. Aim every sentence at that reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide who the intended reader is and adjust level, examples, and explanations accordingly; do not attempt to write for everyone at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize first (outline before prose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize first. Spend a long time on the outline. Decide the order of theorems, lemmas, definitions, examples before writing prose. Reorganization is the bulk of writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work out structure and sequence — the order of results and explanations — prior to drafting full sentences; expect to reorganize repeatedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the spiral plan (pedagogical order over strict logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The spiral plan. Don't present material in strict logical order — that is unreadable. Use the 'spiral' method: introduce concept A loosely, then B, then return to A in more depth, etc. Logical order ≠ pedagogical order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce ideas informally first and revisit them with increasing depth; balance logical rigor with reader accessibility and learning progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every sentence must communicate (no filler)
rubrics_metrics.description: Say something. Every sentence must communicate. Avoid filler, throat-clearing, and meta-commentary about what you are about to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate sentences that do not add information; avoid sentences that only announce structure without content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use complete sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Speak in complete sentences. Mathematical symbols sit inside English sentences. Read your text aloud — if it doesn't parse, fix it. Never start a sentence with a symbol; never abut two formulas with no word between.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure formulas are embedded in grammatical English; read aloud to check parsing; always include connecting words between formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer words to symbols when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Use words, not symbols. Where a word will do, prefer the word. Reserve symbols for the parts that genuinely need precision. Excessive notation is the most common defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit notation to what is necessary for clarity; overuse of symbols burdens the reader. Use words to explain intent and intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose words carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the right words. Distinguish 'any' / 'every' / 'all' / 'some' carefully. Avoid the ambiguous 'any'. Distinguish 'we' from 'I' from 'the reader' with intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise with quantifiers and pronouns; sloppy word choice leads to ambiguity in mathematical statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reusing symbols / resist symbolic pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist symbols. Avoid pronouns of formulas (using a single symbol for two different things in nearby sentences). Don't reuse a symbol for two purposes inside one paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep symbol usage local and unambiguous; avoid shorthand references to formulas that confuse referents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use consistent notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use consistent notation. Pick one letter type for one type of object (lowercase Latin for points, uppercase for sets, Greek for ordinals, etc.) and never deviate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish conventions early and adhere to them throughout the document; consistency aids reader comprehension and memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pronouns and unclear references
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid pronouns and unclear references. 'It', 'this', 'that' must always have an unambiguous referent within reading distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure every pronoun clearly points to a specific, nearby noun or phrase; otherwise replace with explicit references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Write in the active voice when possible. Use 'we' rather than passive constructions. Avoid 'It is shown that...'; prefer 'We show that...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active constructions make exposition clearer and more engaging; use 'we' to guide the reader through arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write good English first
rubrics_metrics.description: Write good English first. Mathematical writing is a subset of English writing. Strunk & White applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend to general principles of good prose (clarity, brevity, coherence) before focusing on mathematical formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use present tense for mathematical statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the present tense. Theorems are eternally true; describe them in the present tense ('Let G be a group', not 'Let G have been a group').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer present-tense narration for definitions, theorems, and statements of fact to reflect their timelessness and improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate definitions and steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the reader what you are doing and why. Start each section with motivation. Don't drop a definition without explaining what problem it solves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context and motivation before formal definitions or technical steps; explain why a concept or result matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the theorem before the proof
rubrics_metrics.description: State the theorem first; then prove it. Don't make the reader guess what is being proved during the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the goal explicit before presenting arguments; avoid burying the statement within the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose mnemonic and conventional notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose notation that helps the reader. Mnemonic letters; respect tradition. Don't call a function f if every other reader has called the same function φ for fifty years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer notation that aligns with reader expectations or mnemonic associations; conserve novelty for when it aids clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'obviously/clearly/trivially' without justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'obviously', 'clearly', 'trivially'. Either prove it or genuinely show why it is obvious by giving the argument briefly. These words are often signs of a gap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a step may not be immediate to the intended reader, supply at least a sketch; use caution with rhetorical shortcuts that mask missing arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-reference precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-reference clearly. Theorem 3.4.1 is better than 'as shown above'. Make it possible to read the paper out of order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use numbered references to results, equations, and sections so readers can locate supporting material when reading selectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate reader confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate reader confusion. Imagine the reader stopping at every sentence and asking 'what?'. Pre-emptively answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactively address likely questions and confusions; insert clarifying remarks or reminders where readers commonly stumble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid novelty/jokes in notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist 'cute' notation, jokes, puns. They date badly and trip the non-native English reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor timeless, clear notation over clever but potentially confusing devices; be mindful of international readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise repeatedly
rubrics_metrics.description: Revise. Then revise again. Halmos rewrote each paper at least six times. The first draft is for the writer; later drafts are for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan multiple revision passes focusing first on structure, then clarity, then sentence-level polish; view early drafts as private thinking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary repetition but reinforce key points
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't repeat yourself, but do reinforce. Vary phrasing; remind the reader of definitions used long ago.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strike a balance between concision and helpful reminders: avoid verbatim repetition but recap essential definitions or results when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft strong opening sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sentence matters most. Spend disproportionate effort on the opening sentence of every section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use openings to set motivation and orientation; a clear, informative first sentence anchors the reader's expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include examples, preferably before abstract statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Include examples. A theorem without an example to anchor it is opaque. Examples should come before the abstract statement when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete examples or special cases to build intuition prior to presenting general theorems or definitions.
